newsitem.title: GERMANY: Lebanese refugee acquitted of Luebeck hostel arson.
newsitem.headline: Lebanese refugee acquitted of Luebeck hostel arson.

text.p: A court in the German port city of Luebeck acquitted a 21-year-old Lebanese refugee, Safwan Eid, on Monday of starting a fire 18 months ago in an asylum-seekers' hostel that killed 10 residents and injured 38.
The fire, in January 1996, was the worst ever to hit a foreigners' home in Germany and raised fears of a renewed wave of neo-Nazi attacks like one that swept the country after unification in 1990.

Eid, a civil war refugee who had lived in the hostel in the north German city with his family for six years, was arrested shortly after the blaze on suspicion of seeking revenge in a quarrel with another resident.
He was later charged with aggravated arson and causing bodily harm. Prosecutors in the nine-month trial called for his acquittal earlier this month citing their own lack of evidence.
Presiding Judge Rolf Wilcken agreed in his verdict that the trial had failed to prove Eid's guilt.

Eid had always protested his innocence. Members of his family and other supporters in the courtroom cheered when they heard the verdict. Eid, who spent seven months in custody, was awarded compensation by the court for his time in jail.
The fire killed six people from the former Zaire, a man from Benin, a Lebanese and a woman from Angola and her six-year-old daughter.

After judge Wilcken read out the verdict, the mother of one of the victims swore at Eid in Arabic and collapsed in sobs. She was one of several victms' relatives who had mounted a private case against Eid alongside state prosecutors.

Wilcken criticised both defence and lawyers representing these co-complainants for using the trial for political ends, he said: "This was particularly inappropriate with regard to the victims of these horrible events".
Anti-racist and left-wing groups launched a huge campaign in Luebeck for Eid's release. They argued the fire was a neo-Nazi attack and the accused was a victim.
But Wilcken also criticised state prosecutors for fuelling media speculation they would mount an appeal to get a re-trial and persuade the court rethink its decision to reject certain evidence.
State prosecutors had based their case on three words Eid allegedly told a first aid worker after he was rescued during the night of the blaze: "It was us".

Eid, however, told the court that what he really said was: "It was them -- they set the stairs on fire," repeating something his father had just told him and said it was obvious his father was talking about a neo-Nazi attack.
State prosecutors argue the court should have permitted them to use conversations between Eid and family members during his time in custody as evidence against him.

But the court rejected the taped conversations which prosecutors said would convict the Lebanese as impermissible evidence on the grounds that they were recorded secretly. Prosecutors have a week to decide whether to appeal.
Eid's defence team argued that prosecutors did not properly investigate four youths, including a skinhead from a local far-right group, who were detained near the scene.
Three of the young men, driving a stolen car, had singed hair. But police accepted their alibis and released them.
